content: The cereal-based product, Super Cereal Plus, was specifically designed for infants and young children (IYC). Annex 5 provides a detailed discussion on the sources of nutrient composition data used for modeling fortified products. To ensure accuracy, all food items in the list were matched to appropriate food composition data. Food composition databases vary significantly across countries in terms of the number of nutrients included, measurement units, sampling standards, analytical methods, and documentation. Currently, there is no comprehensive global food composition database. As of November 16, 2021, we downloaded all available food composition databases from the FAO archive. We did not conduct additional searches for national food composition databases. Additionally, we utilized the Optifood internal food composition database, developed for previous studies, and several project-specific databases provided by colleagues. Given the scope of our project, we selected the U.S. food composition data as the primary source for practical reasons. When food items on our list lacked a suitable match in the U.S. data, we supplemented the data with information from other countries, primarily Germany, for unfortified or unenriched items. If no suitable match was found in either of the two U.S. databases, we searched other databases in a prioritized order: national food composition databases from the relevant country, regional databases (e.g., West African and Southeast Asian databases), the Optifood internal database, FAO global biodiversity and fish food composition databases, project-specific databases, and, if necessary, a national database from a neighboring country. For example, nutrient data for fresh mangosteen and rambutan fruits, which were reported in several Asian studies but absent in U.S. databases, were sourced from the ASEAN food composition database. The final food item list included 404 items representing foods consumed by IYC in one or more of the 37 countries for which we had food item lists. However, 24 of these items lacked sufficient specificity to match them to nutrient values (e.g., if the data source indicated only fish). Consequently, the food composition database included 380 unique nutrient value sets. Once the food item list was compiled and matched to appropriate food composition data, subgroup nutrient profiles were calculated. Food items were first aggregated across all sources and then collapsed to unique items within each country. The mean nutrient value for each nutrient within each food subgroup was calculated, weighted by the number of countries in which each item was consumed. This self-weighting ensured that widely consumed items, such as carrots (reported in 27 of 37 countries), had greater influence on the nutrient profile than less commonly consumed items, such as pumpkin (reported in 15 of 37 countries). Draft nutrient profiles were reviewed to identify and address any undue influence of nutrient outliers within each food subgroup. In a few cases, food composition data were replaced with values from alternative sources, or nutrient values were coded as missing if deemed implausible. Annex 6 provides further details on this process. The review also led to adjustments in the food subgroups due to high heterogeneity or the presence of outliers. For instance, the organ meats subgroup was narrowed to include only liver, and the fish and seafood subgroup was narrowed to include only fish. Excluded items, such as organ meats other than liver and seafood (e.g., crustaceans, bivalves, cephalopods, and snails), were rarely consumed in most countries for which we had data. Nutrient profiles were calculated for foods as consumed, except for whole grains, refined grains, and legumes, for which dry forms were used due to variability in water content. Retention factors were applied to account for nutrient losses during cooking, ensuring that the profiles reflected retention-adjusted dry forms. For analyses exploring single staple foods, specific items were selected for rice-based and maize-based diets, while the nutrient profile for roots, tubers, and plantains was used. Data on the prevalence of consumption and daily intakes in grams informed the specification of Optifood modeling parameters for maximum quantities and frequencies of consumption for food groups and subgroups. Survey weights were applied when available and appropriate. For each dataset, items were coded into food subgroups, and yield factors were applied as needed before collapsing the files to the food subgroup level. Prevalence of consumption and median daily intakes in grams were determined for each food subgroup, and these data were used to inform parameter selection. Optifood modeling required defining parameters such as median grams per day (daily servings), maximum days per week a food subgroup could be consumed, and maximum daily servings per week at the broader food group level. Modeling was conducted on a weekly basis rather than daily. For most food subgroups, maximum quantities and frequencies were set to reflect feasible but generous amounts to maximize the possibility of meeting nutrient needs. Exceptions included fluid milk for breastfed infants, where parameters were set after consultation with WHO staff to address concerns about displacement of breast milk. In summary, maximum daily serving sizes in grams for each food subgroup were based on median gram intakes in countries with the highest consumption. Maximum days per week for food subgroup consumption were estimated based on prevalence in the country with the highest prevalence, using the method of Skau et al. (2014). Maximum daily servings per week for food groups were estimated by extrapolating from the number of subgroups consumed on the recall day. Annex 7 provides detailed information on these calculations.
